cases.n: Brazil — Joint Congressional Inquiry (CPMI) into networks sexually exploiting children (2004)
cases.who: Networks including politicians, businessmen, judges and clergy named by the commission
cases.d: A joint commission of 11 senators and 11 deputies, created in 2003 to investigate violence and networks of sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, received more than 800 complaints and heard about 300 people in 14 states. Its final report, approved on 13 July 2004, put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians (one federal deputy, two state deputies and three mayors), about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed the cases to federal and state prosecutors. It recommended reclassifying 'offences against public morals' as sexual crimes and making internal trafficking of adolescents a crime.
cases.cite: Relatório final da Comissão Parlamentar Mista de Inquérito da exploração sexual de crianças e adolescentes (Senator Patrícia Saboya, president; Deputy Maria do Rosário, rapporteur), 2004; Senate speech of Sen. Patrícia Saboya, 12 May 2004; Al Jazeera, 17 July 2004

cases.n: Brazil — Senate 'CPI da Pedofilia' on online abuse material and child abuse (2008–2010)
cases.who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; a Pará state deputy convicted after testimony
cases.d: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years and delivered a final report of about 1,700 pages to the Federal Police and federal prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and that a state deputy from Belém was convicted and jailed for abusing children after testifying. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and closed businesses where children were exploited.
cases.cite: Federal Senate, CPI da Pedofilia final report (December 2010), as reported by Rádio Senado, 13 and 16 December 2010

cases.n: Brazil — Chamber of Deputies inquiry asks indictment of 37, including a mayor and state deputies (2014)
cases.who: Local politicians and others in Amazonas, Minas Gerais and other states
cases.d: A parliamentary inquiry of the Chamber of Deputies, installed in 2012 with Deputy Liliam Sá as rapporteur, approved its final report on 4 June 2014. It asked for the indictment of 37 people for sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, among them the mayor of Coari (Amazonas), Adail Pinheiro, a serving Amazonas state deputy, a former state deputy and a former president of the Três Corações city council.
cases.cite: Câmara dos Deputados, CPI Exploração Sexual de Crianças e Adolescentes, final report approved 4 June 2014, as reported by Congresso em Foco

cases.n: Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984)
cases.victims_note: report: no fewer than 200 children under 15 kidnapped; 8,961 disappearances recorded in all
cases.who: Argentine armed and security forces (1976–83)
cases.cover: Identities of children changed; records of births in detention not kept
cases.d: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,961 forced disappearances and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and handed to military families. The report was the first official finding of the practice later judged a 'systematic plan' in 2012.
cases.cite: Comisión Nacional sobre la Desaparición de Personas, Nunca Más, 20 September 1984 (via Wikipedia and Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture)

cases.n: Chile — National Prosecutor's Office: 166 investigations of clergy and church workers, 248 victims (2019)
cases.victims_note: 131 of the 248 were children or adolescents when abused; 35 adults; no information for 82
cases.who: Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers; 10 bishops investigated
cases.d: After the 2018 Scicluna mission, Chile's National Prosecutor's Office opened a national review of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church, with raids on diocesan offices. Its balance of 30 April 2019 counted 166 open or closed investigations, 221 people investigated, including 10 bishops (mostly for alleged cover-up), and 248 victims, of whom 131 were children or adolescents.
cases.cite: Fiscalía Nacional de Chile, balance of investigations into members of the Catholic Church, 30 April 2019, as reported by El Dínamo

cases.n: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
cases.who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
cases.cover: Hospital birth records for 1970–1990 missing or destroyed
cases.d: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, who were frequently told their babies had died, and sent for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff and Civil Registry staff, and that private intermediaries were the main channel and were paid. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report in October 2019.
cases.cite: Cámara de Diputados de Chile, Comisión Especial Investigadora sobre adopciones irregulares, report of July 2019 (approved October 2019), as reported by El Desconcierto

cases.n: Ecuador — National Assembly 'AAMPETRA' commission on sexual violence in schools (2018)
cases.victims_note: named after the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari in Quito, where 41 children were abused; government data later showed 4,221 pupils suffered sexual violence in schools 2014–May 2020 (HRW analysis)
cases.who: Teachers and staff of public and private schools; Ministry of Education
cases.cover: Commission found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities
cases.d: Ecuador's National Assembly set up a multiparty occasional commission in 2017 after families of pupils abused at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari (AAMPETRA) in Quito, where 41 children were abused, mobilised. It reviewed cases from 2013 to 2017 and, in a report approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities and concluded that former ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch's later analysis of government data counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.
cases.cite: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador, Comisión Especializada Ocasional AAMPETRA, report approved 16 February 2018; Human Rights Watch, 9 December 2020

cases.n: Jamaica — Keating Report on children in state care finds sexual abuse by caregivers (2003)
cases.who: Jamaican children's homes and places of safety; Child Services Division
cases.cover: Nine of 15 homes visited could not recall an official inspection in the previous three years
cases.d: The Government of Jamaica appointed a four-member review panel chaired by Sadie Keating in December 2002, after a public campaign about abuse in children's homes. Its report, made public in July 2003, found that children in homes and places of safety had been sexually abused, including by care-givers, and that nine of the 15 homes visited could not recall a Child Services Division inspection in three years.
cases.cite: Report on the Situation of Children in the Care of the Jamaican State (Keating Report), 2003, as reported by the Jamaica Observer, 15 July 2003

cases.n: Trinidad and Tobago — Sabga task force on children's homes, kept secret for 25 years
cases.victims_note: 30 to 40 children abused by one employee at St Dominic's Children's Home
cases.who: Children's homes incl. St Dominic's Children's Home and St Jude's School for Girls
cases.cover: Abuser at St Dominic's was asked to resign and allegedly helped into hospital work; report never published by government
cases.d: A task force appointed by the Cabinet in 1997 and chaired by Robert Sabga visited nine children's homes. It found that a male employee at St Dominic's Children's Home had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children and, when discovered, was asked to resign and allegedly helped to find work at a hospital; it also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls. The report was never published; the Trinidad Express published its findings in May 2022.
cases.cite: Report of the Cabinet-appointed Task Force on children's homes (Robert Sabga, chair), 1997, as published by the Trinidad Express, May 2022

cases.n: Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022)
cases.victims_note: 16,238 documented recruited children 1990–2017; estimated 27,101–40,828 with under-reporting; recruitment figure, not a count of sexual-violence victims
cases.who: FARC-EP, ELN and other guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and state security forces (recruitment and use of minors)
cases.d: Colombia's Commission for the Clarification of Truth published its volume on children and adolescents, 'No es un mal menor', in July 2022. It documented 16,238 children recruited by armed groups between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828, and described recruitment as intentional and systematic, including use of minors by the state security forces. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception at an early age, forced to have abortions, and subjected to harassment, rape and sexual torture, and that boys suffered some of these abuses less often.
cases.cite: Comisión para el Esclarecimiento de la Verdad, Informe Final, 'No es un mal menor: Niñas, niños y adolescentes en el conflicto armado', July 2022

cases.n: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004)
cases.victims_note: 2,058 abductions of women and girls reported to the TRC; 189 allegations of sexual slavery (72.5% attributed to the RUF, 11.6% to the AFRC)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF), Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Civil Defence Forces (CDF), Sierra Leone Army, West Side Boys
cases.d: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone presented its final report to the UN Security Council on 5 October 2004. It found that all armed groups targeted girls, and that the RUF and the AFRC 'deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years', using them as sexual and domestic slaves and 'wives'; in a few cases the children were under ten. It also found that the CDF pursued a strategy of rape and sexual slavery against girls and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex. Of 2,058 abductions of women and girls reported to it, and 189 allegations of sexual slavery, most were attributed to the RUF.
cases.cite: Witness to Truth: Report of the Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2004), chapter 'Women and the Armed Conflict' (excerpts compiled by McMaster University Truth Commissions Digital Collection); Wikipedia

cases.n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — RUF leaders convicted of sexual slavery, forced marriage and use of child soldiers (2009)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF): Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, Augustine Gbao
cases.d: On 25 February 2009 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted RUF leaders Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon on 16 of 18 counts and Augustine Gbao on 14, including sexual slavery and the enlistment of child soldiers; all three were convicted of forced marriage, the first such convictions by an international criminal court. They were sentenced on 8 April 2009 to 52, 40 and 25 years, and the appeals were dismissed on 26 October 2009.
cases.cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Sesay, Kallon and Gbao (RUF case), Trial Judgment 25 February 2009; Appeal Judgment 26 October 2009 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.place: Freetown (Special Court; trial held in The Hague)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; RUF and AFRC forces he aided
cases.d: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts, on the basis of aiding and abetting the RUF and AFRC, including sexual slavery and conscripting or enlisting children under 15. He was sentenced to 50 years on 30 May 2012, and the appeal judgment was given on 26 September 2013.
cases.cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Charles Ghankay Taylor, Trial Judgment 26 April 2012 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: South Africa — Human Rights Commission finds sexual abuse in schools systemic (2026)
cases.place: Johannesburg (SAHRC); complaint from St John's College, Mthatha
cases.victims_note: SACE recorded 826 sexual misconduct complaints against educators 2021–2025; 9,857 child sexual abuse cases recorded nationally in 2024/25 (all settings)
cases.who: Educators and other adults in South African schools; South African Council for Educators; education departments
cases.cover: Dismissed educators not automatically deregistered or placed on the safeguarding register; a shortfall of 10,748 convicted offenders not entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders
cases.d: After a complaint about an alleged sexual offence by an educator at St John's College in Mthatha, the South African Human Rights Commission convened a stakeholder roundtable and on 29 June 2026 released a report describing child sexual abuse in schools as systemic. It recorded 826 sexual misconduct complaints to the South African Council for Educators between 2021 and 2025 and found that labour dismissals do not lead automatically to deregistration or listing on the safeguarding register, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.
cases.cite: South African Human Rights Commission, report on sexual violence at schools ('a crisis of fragmentation, delayed integration and uneven enforcement'), media statement 29 June 2026

cases.n: DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003)
cases.who: All parties: FAC (later FARDC), RCD-G, MLC, RCD-K/ML, RCD-N, UPC and PUSIC, FNI and FRPI, FAPC, Mayi-Mayi, ex-FAR/Interahamwe and others
cases.d: The UN human rights office's Mapping Exercise report, published on 1 October 2010, covered the most serious violations in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described 'the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault allegedly by all combatant forces' against women and girls, including Hutu refugee children in 1996–97, and the widespread use of child soldiers by all parties, who suffered murder, rape and torture in military camps. It listed 12 parties named by the Secretary-General for recruiting children, among them the national army.
cases.cite: OHCHR, Report of the Mapping Exercise documenting the most serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law committed within the territory of the DRC between March 1993 and June 2003, August 2010 (published 1 October 2010)

cases.n: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
cases.victims_note: six boys aged about 8 to 13 interviewed in May–June 2014; further children interviewed in July 2014 (nine) and May 2015 (twelve)
cases.who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
cases.cover: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that more energy went into investigating the leak than the abuse
cases.d: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.
cases.cite: Taking Action on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse by Peacekeepers: Report of an Independent Review on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse by International Peacekeeping Forces in the Central African Republic, 17 December 2015; NPR, 18 December 2015

cases.n: South Sudan — UN Commission finds rape, abduction and sexual slavery of women and girls by armed forces and groups (2022)
cases.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces, opposition forces and armed groups; intercommunal militias
cases.cover: Commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria; court-ordered compensation to victims in Yei unpaid
cases.d: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan presented a report on conflict-related sexual violence to the Human Rights Council on 18 March 2022. It found that parties to the conflict used rape of women and girls as a weapon of terror and political repression, and that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. It noted that a military court in Yei had convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020 but victims had not been paid court-ordered compensation.
cases.cite: UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, conference room paper on conflict-related sexual violence, presented to the Human Rights Council, 18 March 2022, as reported by AllAfrica (UN News)

cases.n: Syria — UN Commission of Inquiry: rape of detained women, girls and boys; forced marriage of girls by ISIS (2018)
cases.who: Syrian government forces and affiliated militias (worst offenders); Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham; Islamic State
cases.d: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic released 'I lost my dignity' on 15 March 2018, based on 454 interviews covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found sexual and gender-based violence pervasive and committed by most parties: women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees including boys were subjected to sexual torture, with government forces and allied militias named as the worst offenders. It found that Islamic State forced girls and women into marriages with its fighters, and that these acts amount to war crimes.
cases.cite: Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic, 'I lost my dignity': Sexual and gender-based violence in the Syrian Arab Republic, A/HRC/37/CRP.3, 15 March 2018 (as reported by VOA)

cases.n: Israel — Kedmi commission on children of Yemenite immigrants who vanished 1948–1954 (2001)
cases.victims_note: about 1,050 babies and toddlers went missing; commission accounting: 972 of 1,033 documented as dead, 5 found alive, 56 unresolved
cases.who: Immigrant transit camps, hospitals and welfare staff in early Israel
cases.d: Israel's third official inquiry, a state commission set up in 1995 and headed from 1999 by Supreme Court Judge Yaacov Kedmi, reported in November 2001 on children of mostly Yemenite immigrants who went missing from transit camps and hospitals between 1948 and 1954. It found most had died, 5 were alive and 56 cases could not be resolved; it rejected a state plot but considered it possible that individual social workers handed children over for adoption. In February 2021 the government expressed sorrow and agreed to pay compensation of €38,000–€50,000 per family.
cases.cite: Commission of Inquiry into the Disappearance of Yemenite Children (Cohen–Kedmi Commission), report November 2001 (via Wikipedia); Irish Times, 23 February 2021

cases.n: Afghanistan — Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014)
cases.who: Powerful men who keep boys for dancing and sexual abuse
cases.cover: Commission called for an end to the 'culture of impunity'; bacha bazi was not then clearly criminalised
cases.d: The Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission concluded a national inquiry into the causes and consequences of bacha bazi, the sexual abuse of boys kept by powerful men to dance, in August 2014. It held 71 focus groups and 17 public hearings in 17 provinces, attended by about 2,200 people, and found that two-thirds of the boys said they received money from the abusers. Its chair, Sima Samar, said the practice was a crime not properly prevented by law and called on the government to fight the culture of impunity.
cases.cite: Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission, Causes and Consequences of Bacha Bazi in Afghanistan (National Inquiry Report), 2014, as reported by the Asia Pacific Forum (21 August 2014) and Anadolu Agency

cases.n: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009)
cases.who: Workers of Malaysian logging companies in Sarawak (no company named)
cases.cover: Sarawak police said three complaints the year before had been probed and none taken to court
cases.d: A team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development investigated in Sarawak in November 2008, and its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that timber workers had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. The team interviewed four women with direct experience and many others who said abuse was common; it named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the previous year without enough evidence to prosecute.
cases.cite: Report of the National Task Force on the sexual abuse of Penan women and girls (Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development), released September 2009, as reported by the Associated Press (via CRIN)

cases.n: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005)
cases.who: Indonesian military; Islamic and other organisations and individuals that took children
cases.d: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were removed from their families and taken to Indonesia between 1975 and 1999, by soldiers who used some as child soldiers or household servants and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called removal of a child from their identity, religion and language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. The joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship also urged a search commission, which was not created.
cases.cite: Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation in Timor-Leste (CAVR), Chega!, 2005, as reported by JusticeInfo.net

cases.n: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.place: New York (UN Headquarters); findings centred on MONUC, Bunia
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.d: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and girls described 'rape disguised as prostitution' in exchange for about $1 to $3, food or jobs. OIOS had substantiated 7 cases fully and 2 more by convincing evidence. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.
cases.cite: A comprehensive strategy to eliminate future sexual exploitation and abuse in United Nations peacekeeping operations, UN doc A/59/710, 24 March 2005

cases.n: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.victims_note: 2024 only: 125 victims in peacekeeping and political missions, 98 adults and 27 children
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.cover: About 750 paternity claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 unresolved; troop-contributing countries mostly took no meaningful action
cases.d: Each year since 2003 the Secretary-General reports to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against implementing-partner staff. It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cite: Report of the Secretary-General, Special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (A/79/789, 2025), as reported by AP via NPR/WHQR, 19 March 2025

notes:
Scope of this file: Checklist 1 for Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa, Middle East, South Asia, East and Southeast Asia, Central Asia and international bodies.
Placement: international-body findings (Zeid 2005, SG annual SEA reports) are placed at UN Headquarters, New York, with iso3 set to the country with most findings (COD) and others in 'also'. Re-code if the map has a convention for international records.
Pakistan Kasur (pak-kasur-2015): the Punjab JIT (Express Tribune, 14 Nov 2015) confirmed 19 genuine sodomy claims of the rumoured 284, examined 47 clips, charged 17 people and recommended 8 of 31 FIRs be discharged as fake. The existing record's 'about 280 children' should carry this JIT figure.
Chile: the Fiscalía count (x-chl-fiscalia-iglesia-2019) is a prosecutor's national tally, not a single report; kept because the brief names prosecutors' findings.
Brazil CPI da Pedofilia (2010): the final report's indictment total was not found; Rádio Senado says only 'hundreds' arrested or indicted.
Brazil CPMI 2004: '250 put on notice' and the breakdown come from Al Jazeera (17 July 2004), not the report PDF itself.
Trinidad and Tobago Sabga task force (1997): the report was never officially published; its content is known from the Trinidad Express (May 2022).
South Africa SAHRC 2026: the report comes from a stakeholder roundtable, not a formal national hearing.
Peru: Congress set up an investigative commission on sexual abuse of minors in institutions, including the Sodalicio (chair Alberto de Belaunde, May 2018, 180-day mandate, later extended). No final report was found, and Congress was dissolved in September 2019. Unconfirmed, so not on the checklist.
Mexico: the Supreme Court's 2007 Article 97 investigation (Cacho case) is listed as excluded. Also not checked: congressional or prosecutorial findings beyond CNDH RecVG 14, the Legion report and the bishops' figures.
Not confirmed, because the web-search budget for this turn ran out before these could be checked: Guatemala CEH (1999) on child disappearances and adoptions (its Wikipedia article gives no child-specific finding); Peru CVR (2003) on sexual violence against girls; Bolivian Jesuit or bishops' commissioned reviews (Pedrajas); Paraguay CVJ; Kenya TJRC (2013); AU Commission of Inquiry on South Sudan (2014); UN Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen; Nepal (Hague Permanent Bureau / UNICEF–Terre des hommes 2008 adoption reports, the latter an NGO report); Bangladesh, China, Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia (KPAI / Komnas Perempuan), Vietnam and Central Asia. I found no official national finding for these in the sources I opened. Central Asia appears to have none; that is a gap, not a confirmed absence.
Liberia TRC: excluded for now. Volume I does not single out child sexual abuse. Volume II (figures) may contain child-specific findings; worth a later check.
ICC Bemba (CAR; trial conviction 2016 including rapes, acquitted on appeal 2018) and Katanga were not added: the findings are not specific to children. The ICC Kony confirmation of charges is not a judgment.
